newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Bad weather seen shrinking Jan US income.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Bad weather seen shrinking Jan US income.

text.p: Americans appear to have continued loading up on consumer goods at a robust pace in January, despite a weather-related drop in their take-home pay, analysts said.
Severe winter storms blasted the West coast in late December and early January, disrupting businesses and shrinking employee wages, analysts noted.

"There was a huge drop in the workweek (2.0 percent) coming out of the January employment report and we had average hourly earnings down 1.9 percent," observed Kenneth Mayland, chief economist at Society National Bank.
"But it's nothing to worry about. It's understood to be purely a weather disruption and I expect we'll see a recovery in hours worked in February," he added.
Analysts generally see consumption having risen by 0.5 percent in January, matching December's figure, while income was at best flat and possibly down by half a percentage point.
The January data debut on Monday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.

Steady spending growth indicated in reports on chain store sales and other retail-oriented series, plus expectations for a significant addition to nonfarm payrolls in February have economists convinced that consumption has continued unabated.

"The consumer continues to add to gross domestic product at a rather fast clip. The data are consistent with the idea that the consumer is still buying," said Christopher Rupkey, financial economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
Rupkey sees consumption boosting GDP by 2.5 percentage points in the first quarter, underpinning solid economic growth going forward.

Despite such solid spending growth, the U.S. economy has not yet seen a significant increase in inflation, which probably allows room for more growth without any need for Federal Reserve interest rate hikes, analysts said.

"Right now we have imports that are probably satisfying the extra demand for goods, and we see that Japanese car makers have been able to sell in the U.S. at attractive prices because of the strength of the dollar against the yen," said Astrid Adolfson, economist at consulant group MCM MoneyWatch.
But Fed officials are probably already worrying about faster inflation, as Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan seemed to suggest in his Congressional testimony on Wednesday, Adolfson added.

"As we go down the road, if demand pressures continue and we get more income growth and people continue to spend, at some point we'll get an inflation impact. Then the Fed will probably have to continue worrying," Adolfson said.
Economists have marveled at the lack of inflation acceleration in the U.S. despite over six years of continuous expansion and an unemployment rate at or below 5.5 percent since May 1995.
But a rapidly growing labor force and heavy industrial capital investment have opened extra space for the economy to grow without straining resources or boosting inflation, analysts said.
"The potential growth rate of the economy may have seen some improvement. Capacity has grown pretty rapidly in the manufacturing sector and maybe the service sector as well," said Mayland.
